# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This report settles more than any of the earlier documents. It holds itself to the standards the critics asked for: a randomised comparison, record-based output, a stricter hours measure, a two-year horizon and a pre-registered mediation test. Its responses to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are fair and well supported. Section 5 also confirms the suspicion from my review of the meta-analysis that its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

The arithmetic checks out:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| 0.966 / 0.88 (timesheets) | +9.8% ✓ |
| 0.966 / 0.89 (logs) | +8.5% ✓ |
| Confidence intervals | centred on the log scale ✓ |
| Halden continuers: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866; 0.968 / 0.866 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 ✓ |

There are five substantive problems. The first could change the main estimate of decline.

## 1. Two control offices changed their practice, which biases the 24-month estimate

The "unplanned observation" is presented as a side finding. It also means part of the control group changed during the trial. Two of the seven control case-processing offices cut meetings in month 15, and their output per hour then rose by 4.1%. That raises the control average, which **shrinks the measured treatment effect** at 24 months.

So part of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from controls improving, not from the treatment effect fading. Taken at face value, the two offices' 4.1% gain over the last nine months would lower the control mean by roughly 2 × 4.1 / 7 ≈ 1.2 points. That is close to half the 2.7-point decline. This is a rough calculation, but it shows the effect is not negligible.

The audit may also not have been independent of the trial. Control staff knew about it, and the meetings finding had been published at nine months. If the audit was prompted by the trial, this is contamination, not an unrelated event.

Recommended:
- Report the 24-month estimates with the two offices excluded, and with their post-audit months excluded.
- Present the decline as possibly overstated.
- Say whether the audit was prompted by the trial's results.

## 2. The summary compares figures on different hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% uses timesheet hours and the 8.5% uses log-in hours. On the same measure the change is 12.5% to 9.8%, as the body correctly states. The summary therefore overstates the decline, from about a fifth to about a third.

The decline is also not statistically established. The nine-month interval (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month interval (4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. Report a test of the difference, and describe the result as "consistent with modest fading" rather than an established decline.

## 3. What the log measure captures, and its baseline

- **Construct.** "Active log-in time on the case-management system" presumably records time spent working on cases, not time in meetings, on the phone, or on other work outside the system. If so, it is not a stricter measure of *total* hours. It is a measure of *case-work* hours. The statement "log data show slightly more work than timesheets" assumes the two measure the same thing.
- **Interaction with the meetings finding.** If treated offices cut meetings by about 3.5 hours a week, much of that time would move into logged case-work. That alone would make logged hours fall by less than total hours, without any hidden work. It also makes the mediation result harder to read. Meetings explaining 47% of the gain in output *per logged case-work hour* implies meetings were reducing the productivity of case-work hours themselves, for example by breaking up the day. That may be true, but it is a different mechanism from "meetings took time away from cases." The report should say which mechanism it has in mind and what the logs include.
- **Baseline.** Log hours appear only at 24 months ("added" at follow-up). A difference-in-differences estimate needs pre-period log data. State whether historical logs were retrieved, and from which period.

## 4. The mediation analysis

The registered test is a real improvement and answers the "post hoc" objection directly. Some caveats are still needed:

- **Source of the meeting baseline.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. My review of it noted there was no baseline. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). State how they were obtained, for example retrieved retrospectively from calendar history, and whether the retrieval method was the same for both arms.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds precision only if office-months are treated as independent, and they are not. The effective sample is still 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% for a proportion mediated looks narrow for 14 clusters. Confirm that the standard errors are clustered by office, preferably with a method designed for few clusters.
- **Correlated mediators.** Fewer meetings plausibly reduce fatigue. With two correlated mediators, the share assigned to each depends on how the model is specified. Report the model, and preferably the shares under other specifications.
- **"Confirms" is too strong.** The limitations section rightly notes the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption. The summary should match: "supports" or "is consistent with."

## 5. The Halden subset

- **Selection.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations responded. This is a further selection step on top of the two the report acknowledges, so the subset is selected three times over. The non-responders' sectors and 6-month results should be reported.
- **"Upper bound."** Without a comparison group, this figure is not a formal bound. General economic conditions could push it either way. "Likely to overstate" is accurate.
- **Comparison with earlier figures.** The continuers' 96.8 cannot be compared with Varga and Holm's 95.4 at month six, because the sets of organisations differ. The report doesn't make this comparison, but readers may, so a sentence warning against it would help.
- **The marketing agency reversion.** A marketing agency is discretionary work in the meta-analysis's coding, and it reverted, citing client deadlines. Grouping it under "client-facing or coverage obligations" glosses over this. It suggests that external deadlines can tie discretionary work to time in much the same way coverage does. It is one organisation, but it is worth a sentence.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Counter-arm costs.** A 12% increase in staff raising cost per contact by 9% implies staff are about 75% of total cost. State that assumption.
- **Few-cluster inference.** This is still unaddressed from the nine-month report. Randomisation inference with 7 v 7 offices is straightforward.
- **Backlog.** Output per employee at −3.4% over two years could add up to a growing backlog. Report backlog size and time to decision against statutory deadlines. This was also missing at nine months.
- **Quality and resignations.** The overturn rates (3.2% v 3.0%) and resignation rates have no intervals.
- **The energy extrapolation.** The report repeats "zero by month ten." By my calculation, Varga and Holm's own straight-line extrapolation reaches zero at about month 8.7. This doesn't affect the rebuttal, but the figure shouldn't be repeated uncorrected.
- **Independence.** The follow-up's authors include the Varden authors, who proposed the meetings hypothesis, and a Halden author whose pilot the re-analysis criticised. Pre-registration reduces the concern. A conflict-of-interest statement, and ideally an independent replication of the mediation analysis on the shared data, would strengthen the conclusions.

## Overall

The report's main conclusions hold:

- A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years in randomised, record-based, actual-hours data.
- The "entirely an artifact" claim is refuted.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on inadequate studies.
- Coverage-bound work cannot sustain reduced hours without extra staff.

The main corrections are to reframe the decline, which is overstated in the summary and possibly inflated by control-office contamination, and to clarify what the log measure captures, since that bears on how to read both the hours correction and the meetings mediation. The report's closing caution is also well taken: no arm reorganised work without cutting hours. Whether reorganisation alone could deliver most of the gain is the obvious design for the next trial.
